documents.title: EURETINA guidelines for management of retinal vein occlusion

chunks.content: Introduction Retinal vein occlusion (RVO) leads to visual loss second only to diabetic retinopathy. Its pathogenesis is mainly retinal vein stenosis or relaxation restriction, which, in turn, causes blood flow block or intravascular thrombosis. Retinal vein occlusion can be divided into central RVO (CRVO) and branch RVO (BRVO) [ ]. Worldwide, the prevalence of BRVO is approximately 0.4%, compared with 0.08% for CRVO, and is evenly distributed between men and women, with a higher risk in the elderly population [ ]. Macular oedema (MO), a leading cause of visual impairment, can occur with either CRVO or BRVO [ ]. The pathomechanism involves increased venous blood pressure and damage to the vessel wall, leading to fluid leakage [ ]. The accurate diagnosis and monitoring of RVO–MO have been revolutionised by advances in ocular imaging, particularly optical coherence tomography (OCT). Optical coherence tomography provides high-resolution, cross-sectional visualisation of retinal pathology, allowing clinicians to localise and delineate the extent of MO, detect associated features such as disorganisation of retinal inner layers (DRIL) or hyperreflective foci and objectively quantify central retinal thickness (CRT). These precise anatomical biomarkers are indispensable not only for diagnosis and treatment decisions with current therapies but also for defining the eligible patient population and treatment endpoints for emerging modalities, such as gene therapy [ – ]. Recently, research has focused on using anti-inflammatory and anti-vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) therapeutic strategies to reduce MO and improve vision. Two established treatments are widely used in clinics: intravitreal ranibizumab (RNZ; Lucentis; Genentech, Inc., South San Francisco, CA, USA) and intravitreal dexamethasone (DEX; Ozurdex ® ; Allergan plc, Dublin, Ireland) implants, both of which have been approved for the treatment of RVO with MO in several countries [ ]. Dexamethasone sustained-release implants are coated with the Novadur ® solid polymer matrix (Allergan plc/AbbVie Inc.) containing the glucocorticoid DEX. The implant is injected into the vitreous cavity through the pars plana using a proprietary 22-gauge applicator. One study showed that DEX is present in the retina and vitreous for up to 6 months and reaches peak concentrations in the first 2 months after injection [ ]. Another study compared a 0.7-mg DEX vitreous implant, a 0.35-mg DEX implant and a sham injection for the treatment of MO secondary to BRVO and CRVO, revealing that DEX vitreous implants significantly reduced the risk of visual loss [ ]. In addition, a randomised controlled trial (RCT) of MO secondary to RVO found that a 0.7-mg DEX vitreous implant significantly improved visual acuity and anatomical outcomes in Chinese patients, and both best-corrected visual acuity (BCVA) and CRT were better than sham injections within 3–4 months after a single DEX treatment [ ]. However, as a long-acting steroid preparation, DEX has some potential side effects, such as cataracts and glaucoma, which are more likely to occur at > 6 months of treatment and may require additional intraocular surgery, which can be regarded as a limitation of this treatment approach [ ]. At present, intravitreal injection of anti-VEGF, such as RNZ, bevacizumab and pegaptanib sodium, has become the main treatment for RVO complicated with MO [ , ]. However, due to its short half-life and short-acting effect, repeated injections are necessary after the effective concentration has been reduced. This not only increases the financial burden on patients but also introduces risks, such as infection and glaucoma, caused by intraocular injection [ ]. Based on the above research status, there are clearly many treatment methods for RVO complicated with MO. The most common treatment methods are intravitreal anti-VEGF drugs and intravitreal steroid drugs; however, it remains clinically challenging to determine which of these two treatment methods should be used [ ]. This is because the decision involves balancing their distinct profiles – anti-VEGF agents (e.g. RNZ) often provide rapid visual improvement but require frequent injections, whereas steroids (e.g. DEX implants) offer sustained therapy with fewer injections but carry a higher risk of elevated intraocular pressure (IOP) and cataract progression [ – ]. Ranibizumab and DEX implants are two of the more commonly used anti-VEGF and intravitreal steroid drugs, and many separate clinical trials have confirmed their effectiveness. At present, only the results of single studies comparing the two therapeutic effects are available [ – ]. This study adopts a meta-analysis method to compare the efficacy of RNZ and DEX, providing evidence-based advice for the selection of clinical treatment methods. Therefore, this study collects the published literature and quantifies the clinical effect and safety of these two treatments systematically through a meta-analysis. Therefore, this study collects the published literature and quantifies the clinical effect and safety of these two treatments systematically through a meta-analysis. Data and methods Literature search Following the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses guidelines, the research team conducted a systematic search. The search cutoff date was 31 August 2025. During the search, subject headings and free words were combined for the queries. The search terms were as follows: (1) ‘retinal vein occlusion’ OR ‘retinal vein thrombosis’ OR ‘branch retinal vein occlusion’ OR ‘central retinal vein occlusion’; (2) ‘macular oedema’; (3) ‘intravitreal dexamethasone implant’ OR ‘dexamethasone’ OR ‘dexamethasone implant’ OR ‘Ozurdex’; and (4) ‘intravitreal ranibizumab’ OR ‘ranibizumab’ OR ‘Lucentis’. Inclusion and exclusion criteria The study type (RCT or retrospective study), participants (age and disease type), interventions (specific drugs and dosage range, such as 0.5 mg of RNZ) and outcome measures (measurement units and time points for BCVA, CRT, etc.) were further clarified. All included studies required quantitative data that could be used for meta-analysis. The inclusion criteria were as follows: (1) study type – RCT or retrospective; (2) study participants – adult patients with BRVO or CRVO complicated with MO (aged ≥ 18 years); (3) interventions – (i) RNZ group (intravitreal RNZ for patients with RVO complicated with MO) or (ii) DEX group (intravitreal DEX implants for patients with RVO complicated with MO); and (4) outcome measures – BCVA, CRT, IOP and number of injections. The exclusion criteria were as follows: (1) patients who had previously received intravitreal injection or laser therapy; (2) patients with complications introduced by other treatment methods; (3) incomplete data; (4) repeated published studies; and (5) reviews, case reports or other studies. Literature screening The literature screening and data extraction process was independently conducted by two researchers (LY and LYH). They were blinded to each other’s assessment results, meaning that they could not see each other’s decisions during the screening and evaluation process to reduce subjective bias. For consistency of the literature screening and data extraction, the inter-rater reliability, using the Kappa statistic for categorical variables (e.g. inclusion/exclusion decisions) and the intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC) for continuous variables (e.g. extracted means, standard deviations) were calculated. The final Kappa value was 0.85, and the ICC values were all > 0.9, indicating excellent consistency between the raters. Any disagreements were resolved through discussion and consultation with a third researcher (ZJ). Literature quality evaluation Two independent researchers assessed the risk. Risk of bias was evaluated using the Cochrane Handbook (version 5.1.0) [ ]. The literature quality was divided into three levels: Level A (completely meeting the criteria), Level B (partially meeting the criteria ) and Level C (not meeting the criteria). In case of disagreement, a third investigator was consulted to reach an agreement. For the quality evaluation of retrospective studies, the Newcastle–Ottawa Scale (NOS) [ ] was used, which is scored on three aspects: selection, comparability and exposure or outcome, with 1 point for each condition met and a total score of 9 points. Studies with scores < 5 were of low quality, and studies with scores ≥ 5 were of high quality. Statistical analysis In this study, the RevMan 5.3 statistical software package (The Cochrane Collaboration, London, UK) was used. For dichotomous data, odds ratios were used as effect measures; for continuous data, weighted mean differences (MDs) were used as effect measures, and effect sizes were presented as point estimates with their 95% confidence intervals (CIs). Heterogeneity among included studies was assessed through the heterogeneity test. The test level for meta-analysis was set at α = 0.05. Results Literature search results A total of 385 relevant articles were identified in the databases for this study. Following systematic screening, 10 eligible articles [ – ] were included for meta-analysis and systematic review (Fig. ). Basic characteristics A total of 1,274 patients with RVO complicated with MO treated with intravitreal RNZ or intravitreal DEX implants were included in 10 studies; there were 4 RCTs and 6 retrospective studies. The average age and gender of the patients in the literature were extracted, as well as the follow-up time (see Table ). The 4 RCTs included in this study were all evaluated using the risk assessment tool for bias in RCTs recommended in the Cochrane Handbook, and the quality rating of all the included literature was Level A (see Supplementary Table ). The NOS was used to evaluate the quality of the included retrospective studies, and the scores were 6–8. All the studies were of medium and high quality, which met the inclusion criteria (see Supplementary Table for details). The NOS was used to evaluate the quality of the included retrospective studies, and the scores were 6–8. Results of the meta-analysis Visual acuity changes Best-corrected visual acuity is an important functional index used to measure the effect of vision treatment. A meta-analysis of BCVA changes in patients with CRVO and BRVO complicated with MO was performed, making comparisons with the baseline at each follow-up point. Best-corrected visual acuity in central retinal vein occlusion The results of the pooled analysis of BCVA improvement in patients with CRVO for both treatment modalities are shown in Fig. . The results show that BCVA (based on Early Treatment of Diabetic Retinopathy Study [ETDRS] letters) improved more significantly in patients receiving intravitreal RNZ than in patients with CRVO receiving an intravitreal DEX implant (MD = 4.16, 95% CI: 0.44–7.88, p = 0.03). The subgroup analysis showed that the difference between groups was statistically significant ( p < 0.001), indicating that the follow-up time was the source of heterogeneity among BCVA indicators. Specifically, there was no obvious difference in BCVA improvement between the two treatment modalities at 1 and 12 months, and there was no heterogeneity between the studies at 1 month (MD = 0.93, 95% CI: −1.92 to 3.77, p = 0.52, I ² = 0.0%). At 6 months, however, BCVA improved more in the RNZ group than in the DEX group (MD = 9.51, 95% CI: 6.20–12.82, p < 0.001). Best-corrected visual acuity in branch retinal vein occlusion The results of the pooled analysis of BCVA improvement in patients with BRVO for both treatment modalities are shown in Fig. . The pooled analysis showed that, overall, there was no significant difference in BCVA improvement between the two treatment groups for BRVO (MD = − 0.04, 95% CI: −0.15 to 0.07, p = 0.49). Subgroup analysis by time points revealed a temporal pattern; RNZ provided superior BCVA improvement in the early phases, with a statistically significant advantage at 1 month (MD = 0.10, 95% CI: 0.04–0.15, p = 0.0004) and 3 months (MD = 0.06, 95% CI: 0.00–0.11, p = 0.03). At later time points (6 and 12 months), the point estimates of the MDs favoured the DEX implant; however, these results were not statistically significant (at 6 months: MD = − 0.15, 95% CI: −0.38 to 0.07, p = 0.18; at 12 months: MD = − 0.13, 95% CI: −0.76 to 0.50, p = 0.68). It is important to note that the results at 6 and 12 months were accompanied by considerable heterogeneity ( I ² = 70% and I ² = 97%, respectively). A subsequent sensitivity analysis by Ozkaya [ ] confirmed that RNZ significantly improved BCVA in patients with BRVO. Following exclusion, the heterogeneity decreased by 4%, and the heterogeneity between groups was statistically significant ( p = 0.003), indicating that the follow-up time was the source of heterogeneity in BCVA in BRVO (see Supplementary Fig. ). Central retinal thickness changes Central retinal thickness represents anatomic changes in the fovea following treatment. In this study, a meta-analysis was performed on the CRT changes in CRVO in patients with BRVO complicated with MO compared with baseline at each follow-up node. Central retinal thickness changes in central retinal vein occlusion The pooled analysis showed that both treatments reduced CRT in patients with CRVO (Fig. ). Patients with CRVO treated with intravitreal RNZ had a greater reduction in CRT (MD = − 106.04, 95% CI: −203.12 to − 8.97, p = 0.03). Patients with CRVO in the RNZ-treated group had a more significant reduction in CRT at 6 months (MD = − 158.83, 95% CI: −270.08 to − 47.57, p = 0.005), but there was high heterogeneity between studies ( I ² = 66.0%). However, at 12 months, there was no difference in CRT reduction between the two treatment modalities (MD = − 31.75, 95% CI: −131.49 to 67.99, p = 0.53). Hoerauf’s sensitivity analysis [ ] demonstrated that RNZ significantly reduced CRT in patients with CRVO. Following exclusion, the heterogeneity decreased to 0% (see Supplementary Fig. ). Central retinal thickness changes in branch retinal vein occlusion The pooled analysis showed that both treatments reduced CRT in patients with BRVO, as shown in Fig. ; there was significant heterogeneity among studies ( I ² = 92.0%). The results showed that patients with BRVO treated with intravitreal RNZ had a significantly greater reduction in

CRT reduction between the two treatment modalities (MD = − 31.75, 95% CI: −131.49 to 67.99, p = 0.53). Hoerauf’s sensitivity analysis [ ] demonstrated that RNZ significantly reduced CRT in patients with CRVO. Following exclusion, the heterogeneity decreased to 0% (see Supplementary Fig. ). Central retinal thickness changes in branch retinal vein occlusion The pooled analysis showed that both treatments reduced CRT in patients with BRVO, as shown in Fig. ; there was significant heterogeneity among studies ( I ² = 92.0%). The results showed that patients with BRVO treated with intravitreal RNZ had a significantly greater reduction in CRT than those treated with an intravitreal DEX implant (MD = − 41.25, 95% CI: −81.44 to − 1.05, p = 0.04). The subgroup analysis showed that the differences between groups were statistically significant ( p < 0.0001), indicating that the follow-up time was the source of heterogeneity in the CRT changes. Central retinal thickness decreased more significantly in the RNZ group than in the DEX group at 3 months (MD = − 92.10, 95% CI: −123.12 to − 61.08, p < 0.001) and 6 months (MD = − 67.01, 95% CI: −113.44 to − 20.59, p = 0.005). The substantial heterogeneity observed in this analysis may be attributed to several factors, including differences in study design (RCTs vs. retrospective studies), variations in the treatment protocols (e.g. fixed dosing vs. pro re nata regimens for RNZ) and diversity in patient baseline characteristics, such as the duration of MO and the extent of ischaemia, which were not consistently reported across all included studies. Despite this heterogeneity, the direction of effect consistently favoured RNZ at the 3- and 6-month time points in the subgroup analysis. Treatment-induced intraocular pressure changes in retinal vein occlusion Increased IOP is a common adverse reaction to the treatment of retinal diseases with intravitreal DEX implants and intravitreal RNZ. Figure shows the IOP changes observed with both treatments in this study. At 1 month after initiation of treatment, MD = − 2.98, 95% CI: −5.79 to − 0.17 and p = 0.04; the IOP in the DEX group increased at 3 months (MD = − 2.00, 95% CI: −2.51 to − 1.50, p < 0.001) and 6 months (MD = − 1.04, 95% CI: −2.02 to − 0.05, p = 0.04) and was higher than in the RNZ group. The pooled results of all included studies showed that the IOP increase in the DEX group was higher than that in the RNZ group after treatment (MD = − 1.82, 95% CI: −2.51 to − 1.12, p < 0.001). A sensitivity analysis by Kaldirim [ ] showed that DEX significantly influenced IOP changes resulting from treatment in patients with RVO. Following exclusion, the heterogeneity decreased by 2%, and the heterogeneity between groups was statistically significant ( p = 0.0007), indicating that the follow-up time was the source of heterogeneity (see Supplementary Fig. ). Number of injections used during the treatment of retinal vein occlusion The number of injections required for intravitreal DEX implants and intravitreal RNZ to treat RVO has been of concern to clinicians. This study analysed the number of injections after 6 and 12 months of RVO treatment included in the articles. The RNZ group received significantly more injections than the DEX group at 6 months (MD = 1.97, 95% CI: 1.38–2.55, p < 0.001) and 12 months (MD = 2.74, 95% CI: 2.31–3.17, p < 0.001) after treatment. The number of injections was higher in the RNZ group than in the DEX group (MD = 2.45, 95% CI: 1.97–2.94, p < 0.001) (see Fig. ). The heterogeneity between groups was statistically significant ( p = 0.04), indicating that the follow-up time was the source of heterogeneity. Publication bias Publication bias analysis was conducted on the above analysis indicators, and no obvious publication bias was found (see Supplementary Figs. – for details). Discussion Ten high-quality articles were included in this study, and the results were reliable. The meta-analysis demonstrated that intravitreal RNZ provided a greater improvement in BCVA and a more significant reduction in CRT than the DEX implant in patients with RVO complicated by MO. Furthermore, postoperative follow-up revealed a higher incidence of elevated IOP in the DEX group. The meta-analysis of this study showed that intravitreal RNZ was superior to intravitreal DEX implants in improving visual acuity in patients with BRVO and CRVO complicated by MO. Specifically, for patients with CRVO, BCVA (based on ETDRS letters) improved more significantly in RNZ-treated patients at 6 months ( p < 0.001). For patients with BRVO, RNZ treatment showed a greater BCVA improvement at 1 month ( p < 0.001) and 3 months ( p = 0.03). These results are consistent with those of previous studies. the DEX group. The meta-analysis of this study showed that intravitreal RNZ was superior to intravitreal DEX implants in improving visual acuity in patients with BRVO and CRVO complicated by MO. Specifically, for patients with CRVO, BCVA (based on ETDRS letters) improved more significantly in RNZ-treated patients at 6 months ( p < 0.001). For patients with BRVO, RNZ treatment showed a greater BCVA improvement at 1 month ( p < 0.001) and 3 months ( p = 0.03). These results are consistent with those of previous studies. For example, the BRAVO study assessed the efficacy and safety of intravitreal RNZ in patients with BRVO complicated by MO and found that 55% and 61% of patients treated with 0.3- and 0.5-mg doses of RNZ achieved a 3-line visual improvement, respectively, compared with only 29% in the control group [ , ]. Anatomically, RNZ was also more effective than the DEX implant in reducing CRT. Patients with BRVO exhibited significant CRT reductions at 3 and 6 months, whereas those with CRVO showed a pronounced effect at 6 months. This suggests that the potent anti-VEGF effect of RNZ leads to a rapid and substantial resolution of MO. The GENEVA study, which compared different DEX doses with sham surgery, supports the concept that the peak effect of steroids may not match the initial powerful anti-oedematous action of anti-VEGF agents [ ]. The observed efficacy of RNZ in our analysis at 6 months, for both BRVO and CRVO, highlights its potent short-to-medium-term activity. Elevated IOP is a well-documented adverse event of intravitreal corticosteroid therapy. Our results consistently showed that IOP was significantly higher in the DEX group than in the RNZ group at 3 and 6 months post-treatment. Clinically, this IOP elevation is often short-term and manageable with topical antihypertensive medications [ , ]. However, vigilant monitoring is essential, as a small subset of patients (e.g. 1.7% in the study by Capone et al. [ ]) may require surgical intervention for glaucoma. Consequently, the safety profile of RNZ regarding IOP is more favourable, although this must be balanced against its higher injection frequency. The injection quantity of intravitreal anti-VEGF drugs and intravitreal steroid drugs for the treatment of RVO has been an ongoing matter of concern; however, related studies have relatively few analyses of the impact of injection frequency on clinical efficacy. The results of the meta-analysis of this study showed that at 6 and 12 months after the start of treatment, the number of injections in the RNZ group was significantly higher than that in the DEX group. The study by Yoon et al. [ ] evaluated the treatment of patients with RVO combined with MO using intravitreal DEX implants. During the 12-month period, 32% and 49% of the patients received one and three injections, respectively. Patients requiring three injections had a higher CRT and larger macular non-perfusion at baseline. In addition, adverse events, such as increased IOP (35%) and newly diagnosed cataracts (16%), occurred. The increased injection frequency of intravitreal RNZ may impose an economic burden and an increased risk of adverse reactions on patients. However, due to the different basic conditions of patients, the choice of treatment methods still needs to be determined based on the patients’ situations. For patients with RVO–MO who already have a high IOP or glaucoma factors, the advantages and disadvantages of the two treatments should be explained to them, and intravitreal RNZ treatment can be recommended. For patients with some economic pressure and no risk factors for glaucoma or cataracts, the advantage of an intravitreal DEX implant lies in the slow and stable release of the drug after a single injection, reducing the safety hazards and economic burden associated with frequent injections. In addition, the DEX implant has been included in the medical insurance reimbursement list for RVO–MO treatment since 2020 in China; therefore, it is a better choice for such patients [ , ]. Our findings can be contextualised by comparing them with the earlier systematic review and meta-analysis by Hu et al. [ ], which also compared intravitreal DEX implants and anti-VEGF agents for the treatment of RVO-related MO. This study, which included 5 RCTs with 873 patients published up to August 2018, concluded that there were no significant differences in BCVA and CRT between the two treatment groups at the primary endpoint, although it noted a substantial reduction in CRT favouring anti-VEGF agents in a subset of studies at 6 months [ ]. Our current meta-analysis builds upon this foundation in several critical aspects. First, we incorporated a more recent and extensive body of literature, including 10 studies (4 RCTs and 6 retrospective studies) with a total of 1,274 patients, almost doubling the sample size and enhancing the statistical power and generalisability of the conclusions. Our current meta-analysis builds upon this foundation in several critical aspects. First, we incorporated a more recent and extensive body of literature, including 10 studies (4 RCTs and 6 retrospective studies) with a total of 1,274 patients, almost doubling the sample size and enhancing the statistical power and generalisability of the conclusions. Second, although Hu et al. [ ] combined different types of RVO (CRVO and BRVO) and different anti-VEGF agents, our study performed detailed subgroup analyses based on the type of occlusion (CRVO vs. BRVO) and specific time points (1, 3, 6 and 12 months), providing a more nuanced and clinically relevant understanding of the differential treatment effects over time. For example, we were able to demonstrate that RNZ was superior to DEX in improving BCVA at 6 months for CRVO and at 1 and 3 months for BRVO and in reducing CRT at 3 and 6 months for both types, findings that were not fully elucidated in the previous meta-analysis. Furthermore, our analysis provided a more comprehensive and quantitative assessment of safety outcomes. We confirmed that the DEX implant was associated with a significantly higher risk of IOP elevation, a finding consistent with that of Hu et al. [ ]. However, we also extended the safety profile comparison by quantitatively analysing the number of injections required, clearly showing that the RNZ group received considerably more injections over 6 and 12 months, which is a crucial factor for treatment burden and healthcare economics. Finally, the inclusion of non-RCT evidence (retrospective studies) in our review, although a limitation in terms of design hierarchy, allows for the incorporation of ‘real-world’ effectiveness data and longer-term outcomes, offering a complementary perspective to that of the rigorous but sometimes restrictive environment of RCTs. In summary, although the core conclusion of Hu et al. [ ] – that both modalities are effective – remains valid, our updated and more extensive analysis provides a finer-grained, temporally resolved and clinically differentiated comparison that can better inform personalised treatment decisions for patients with RVO-related MO. This study has several limitations. The results of the meta-analysis were obtained from different types of research designs, which may have led to bias. Second, a key limitation of our analysis is that most included studies did not stratify outcomes based on the ischaemic subtype of the RVO. Ischaemic status is a known prognostic factor, and the treatment response may differ between ischaemic and non-ischaemic variants. Consequently, our results represent an average effect across these subtypes. Future studies designed to compare RNZ and DEX implants should aim to provide subgroup analyses based on ischaemia to guide more personalised treatment approaches. Third, the potential influence of specific baseline clinical and OCT biomarkers on treatment response could not be assessed in this meta-analysis. Parameters such as lens status (e.g. pseudophakia) or the presence of specific OCT features, such as subretinal fluid (SRF) or DRIL, may predispose patients to a differential response to anti-VEGF therapy versus steroids. For example, patients with pseudophakia may be better candidates for steroid implants due to the eliminated risk of cataract progression. Similarly, the presence of SRF has been suggested in some studies to be associated with a more favourable response to anti-VEGF agents. However, the included studies did not provide stratified outcomes based on these parameters. Therefore, our results represent an average effect across heterogeneous patient profiles. Future studies should aim to analyse whether such biomarkers can serve as predictors for selecting the most effective initial therapy (anti-VEGF or steroid) on an individualised basis. Furthermore, due to the limitation of the follow-up time, the long-term therapeutic effects of the two treatment methods for > 1 year cannot be evaluated. Therefore, it is necessary to incorporate more high-quality, large-sample and long-term follow-up studies in the future to further confirm the value of the results established by the meta-analysis. This would assist in the rational selection of the treatment timing of intravitreal RNZ and intravitreal DEX implants in clinical practice. Although the current standard of care for RVO–MO revolves around repeated anti-VEGF injections or sustained-release steroids, the ultimate therapeutic goal remains achieving durable efficacy with a minimal treatment burden. By directly comparing the two predominant treatment modalities, this meta-analysis provides a robust clinical context for evaluating emerging therapies, notably gene therapy. The findings of this study underscore a fundamental clinical challenge: the trade-off between efficacy and treatment frequency. Ranibizumab, although effective, requires frequent intravitreal injections to maintain its benefits, which poses a considerable burden on patients, caregivers and healthcare systems. current standard of care for RVO–MO revolves around repeated anti-VEGF injections or sustained-release steroids, the ultimate therapeutic goal remains achieving durable efficacy with a minimal treatment burden. By directly comparing the two predominant treatment modalities, this meta-analysis provides a robust clinical context for evaluating emerging therapies, notably gene therapy. The findings of this study underscore a fundamental clinical challenge: the trade-off between efficacy and treatment frequency. Ranibizumab, although effective, requires frequent intravitreal injections to maintain its benefits, which poses a considerable burden on patients, caregivers and healthcare systems. Gene therapy approaches for retinal diseases aim to address this limitation by enabling the sustained endogenous production of anti-angiogenic proteins (e.g. anti-VEGF agents) from a single administration. The efficacy profile of RNZ established in this analysis helps to define the therapeutic benchmark that these novel gene-based treatments must meet or exceed. Furthermore, the sustained anti-inflammatory and anti-oedematous effect observed with the DEX implant, albeit with a different safety profile, provides proof of concept that long-acting therapies are viable and desirable for managing a chronic condition such as RVO–MO. This supports the development rationale for gene therapies designed for sustained expression. Therefore, the results of this meta-analysis not only inform current clinical choices between RNZ and DEX but also contribute valuable comparative data that can guide the design and evaluation of future gene therapy trials, potentially changing the long-term standard of care from chronic reinjection to a one-time treatment. Furthermore, the evolution towards targeted and personalised therapies underscores the critical importance of precise diagnostic biomarkers. The research by Iglicki et al. and other scholars has been instrumental in identifying and validating OCT-based biomarkers (e.g. DRIL and ORYD) that predict treatment response and disease progression in retinal diseases [ , , , ]. The application of these precise imaging criteria for patient selection was a foundational element in the studies we analysed. This approach ensures that the clinical outcomes compared in this meta-analysis are based on a well-defined pathological substrate. For future gene therapy trials, which require meticulous patient stratification and long-term monitoring, the reliance on such objective, quantifiable ancillary tests will be paramount to demonstrate efficacy and ensure that treatment is delivered to those with the precise pathology it aims to address. The findings of this meta-analysis hold substantial practical implications for ophthalmologists worldwide. First, this study provides a synthesised, evidence-based comparison of two fundamental treatment paradigms for RVO–MO: the potent but short-acting anti-VEGF strategy (RNZ) and the sustained-release anti-inflammatory strategy (DEX implant). For ophthalmologists in diverse healthcare settings – from high-volume centres in developed countries to resource-limited environments – this analysis offers critical insights to tailor treatment choices. The superior early visual gains with RNZ may be preferred in settings where frequent monitoring and injection are feasible. Conversely, the sustained efficacy and reduced injection frequency of the DEX implant present a valuable option for patients with limited access to frequent healthcare or those struggling with treatment adherence. This evidence is crucial for optimising individual patient care and for guiding the development of efficient, context-aware treatment protocols on a global scale. Second, by rigorously quantifying the distinct efficacy and safety profiles of each drug over time, this analysis empowers clinicians to make informed decisions and set realistic patient expectations. Understanding that RNZ may offer faster initial results, whereas DEX provides longer-lasting effects with fewer injections but a higher risk of elevated IOP, is essential for shared decision-making. Furthermore, the comprehensive safety comparison alerts clinicians to the necessary postoperative monitoring strategies for each treatment. For readers, this study delivers directly applicable evidence. It moves beyond the results of single trials to provide a consolidated, higher-level conclusion that can be immediately integrated into clinical reasoning. It addresses a common and challenging clinical dilemma with a clear, data-driven narrative, thereby fulfilling the journal’s mission to publish content that has a direct and positive impact on ophthalmic care worldwide. Conclusion Taking the current study evidence together with the results of this meta-analysis, we conclude that intravitreal RNZ is superior to DEX implants in improving BCVA and reducing CRT in patients with RVO complicated by MO. Specifically, RNZ was more effective in improving BCVA and reducing CRT in the early stages of BRVO, whereas it took longer to show efficacy in patients with CRVO. It is important to note that the long-term comparative efficacy (beyond 12 months) of intravitreal RNZ versus the DEX implant remains less defined due to the limited follow-up duration of the included studies. Future large-scale RCTs with longer follow-up periods are warranted to confirm the sustainability of these therapeutic effects and to establish optimal long-term treatment strategies for RVO-associated MO. However, both treatments have their advantages and disadvantages. Future large-scale RCTs with longer follow-up periods are warranted to confirm the sustainability of these therapeutic effects and to establish optimal long-term treatment strategies for RVO-associated MO. However, both treatments have their advantages and disadvantages. For patients with RVO combined with MO treated with intravitreal RNZ, the injection frequency was higher than that of the DEX group, and the duration of therapeutic effect was shorter. Moreover, some of the literature indicates that its improvement in deep vascular complex blood flow is limited [ ]. By contrast, the intravitreal DEX implant requires fewer injections than intravitreal RNZ, has a longer duration of therapeutic effect [ ] and helps reduce the levels of inflammatory factors [ ]. However, it has disadvantages, such as a relatively high risk of elevated IOP, a high risk of secondary glaucoma and a slow onset, which require close attention during the clinical treatment process. For patients with RVO–MO who already have a high IOP or glaucoma factors, intravitreal RNZ treatment can be recommended. For patients with some economic pressure and no risk factors for glaucoma or cataracts, the intravitreal DEX implant reduces safety hazards and the economic burden. Therefore, in clinical practice, exploring the possibility of combined medication and providing targeted medication based on the individual conditions of patients should be the direction for future clinical research.
